question: The primary purpose of wing dihedral, the wings angled upward from root to tip, is to contribute to:

options.text: Longitudinal stability
Lateral (roll) stability, by generating a restoring rolling moment following a sideslip
Directional stability about the vertical axis
A reduction in induced drag

explanation: When a sideslip develops, dihedral causes the lower, into-wind wing to meet the airflow at a slightly higher effective angle of attack than the upper wing, generating more lift on the low wing. This produces a rolling moment back toward wings-level — a lateral, not longitudinal or directional, stabilising effect.

question: The vertical stabilizer (fin) contributes to directional stability mainly through a "weathercock" effect, meaning:

options.text: It generates lift to help support the tail in cruise flight
Following a yaw disturbance, the airflow strikes the fin at an angle and generates a restoring yawing moment back toward the original heading
It reduces the aircraft's roll rate during aileron use
It prevents Dutch roll from ever developing

explanation: If the aircraft yaws away from the direction it is travelling through the air, the fin meets the resulting sideways component of airflow at an angle and generates a sideforce that yaws the nose back to align with the relative airflow — the same principle by which a weathercock aligns with the wind.

question: In a sideslip, a swept wing contributes a stabilising rolling moment similar to dihedral, mainly because:

options.text: The forward wing, into the sideslip, presents a greater effective span perpendicular to the airflow, generating relatively more lift than the trailing wing
Sweepback increases the wing's aspect ratio during a sideslip
The trailing wing always stalls first during a sideslip, rolling the aircraft toward it
Sweepback has no effect on lateral stability, only on critical Mach number

explanation: During a sideslip, the wing swept toward the direction of the slip presents more of its span perpendicular to the oncoming airflow than the trailing wing, effectively increasing its lift compared with the aft wing. This produces a rolling moment back toward wings-level, adding a dihedral-like lateral stabilising effect.

question: "Dutch roll" is a dynamic mode combining:

options.text: Pure roll only, with no yaw
Coupled yawing and rolling oscillation, typically arising when directional (yaw) stability is weak relative to lateral (roll) stability
Pure pitch oscillation
A phenomenon that only affects gliders

explanation: Dutch roll is a coupled yaw-roll oscillation: a yaw disturbance produces a sideslip, dihedral effect rolls the aircraft in response, and that roll feeds back into further yaw. It tends to be more pronounced when an aircraft's lateral (dihedral/sweep) stability is strong relative to its directional (fin) stability, which is common on swept-wing jets.

question: A yaw damper is fitted to many swept-wing jet aircraft mainly to:

options.text: Increase the aircraft's dihedral effect mechanically
Automatically apply small rudder inputs to damp out Dutch roll oscillations, which strong lateral stability relative to directional stability can otherwise leave lightly damped
Trim the aircraft in pitch
Prevent adverse yaw during aileron use

explanation: A yaw damper senses yaw rate and automatically applies small, rapid rudder inputs to damp Dutch roll, a mode that swept-wing aircraft with strong dihedral effect relative to directional stability are otherwise prone to leaving only lightly damped or uncomfortably persistent.

question: An aircraft is said to exhibit "spiral instability" (spiral divergence) if, following a small bank disturbance with controls released, it:

options.text: Returns smoothly to wings-level on its own
Continues to increase bank angle and enters a slowly tightening, steepening turn
Oscillates in roll with constant amplitude indefinitely
Immediately snaps to inverted flight

explanation: Spiral instability arises when directional (yaw) stability is strong relative to lateral (roll) stability: after a bank disturbance, the resulting sideslip yaws the nose further into the turn faster than dihedral can roll the wings back level, so bank angle slowly and progressively increases into a spiral.

question: Aircraft design generally involves a trade-off between lateral (dihedral effect) and directional (fin) stability, because:

options.text: Strong directional stability relative to lateral stability tends to favor spiral stability but can worsen Dutch roll, while the reverse tends to favor Dutch roll damping but worsen spiral stability
The two are always completely independent and never interact
Increasing one always increases the other by an equal amount
Neither has any relationship to the other

explanation: Lateral and directional stability interact rather than acting independently: relatively strong directional stability tends to resist spiral divergence but can leave Dutch roll poorly damped, while relatively strong lateral (dihedral) stability tends to damp Dutch roll but can promote spiral instability — which is why real designs sit at a deliberate compromise, sometimes assisted by a yaw damper.

question: The side area of the fuselage and fin positioned above the aircraft's center of gravity — its "keel surface" — contributes to:

options.text: Longitudinal stability only
Lateral (roll) stability following a sideslip, in a manner similar to dihedral, because the sideways force acts above the center of gravity
Engine cooling only
No aerodynamic effect at all

explanation: During a sideslip, the sideways aerodynamic force on the fuselage side area and fin above the center of gravity produces a rolling moment back toward wings-level, in essentially the same way dihedral does, adding to an aircraft's overall lateral stability beyond its wing geometry alone.

question: All else being equal, a high-wing aircraft generally shows more inherent lateral (dihedral) stability than an equivalent low-wing aircraft, mainly because:

options.text: High wings are always built with more geometric dihedral than low wings
The fuselage hanging below a high wing acts somewhat like a pendulum, and airflow interference in a sideslip adds a further stabilising rolling moment beyond any geometric dihedral
High wings produce inherently more lift than low wings at the same angle of attack
Low-wing aircraft always have anhedral, downward-angled wings

explanation: A high wing's pendulum-like weight distribution below the wing, together with airflow shielding and interference effects around the fuselage during a sideslip, both add a stabilising rolling moment on top of whatever geometric dihedral the wing itself has — which is why high-wing aircraft are often built with little or no additional dihedral, while low-wing aircraft typically need more.

question: "Anhedral" — wings angled downward from root to tip, the opposite of dihedral — is sometimes used on aircraft that already have strong lateral stability from another source, such as significant wing sweep, mainly to:

options.text: Increase lateral stability further
Reduce excessive lateral stability, which can otherwise make an aircraft's roll response feel heavy or contribute to a poorly damped Dutch roll
Increase induced drag intentionally
Improve the stall characteristics only

explanation: Because sweepback itself already provides a dihedral-like stabilising effect, a highly swept wing with additional geometric dihedral could end up excessively laterally stable — sluggish in roll and prone to poorly damped Dutch roll. Some such aircraft use anhedral to bring overall lateral stability back down to a better-balanced level.

question: Left uncorrected, adverse yaw during a roll can interact with dihedral effect because:

options.text: The yaw produces a sideslip, and dihedral effect then rolls the aircraft in response to that sideslip, on top of the roll the ailerons themselves commanded
Dihedral effect eliminates adverse yaw entirely on its own
The two effects are completely unrelated and never interact
Adverse yaw only occurs on aircraft with zero dihedral

explanation: Adverse yaw's momentary sideslip is exactly the trigger dihedral effect responds to, producing an additional rolling moment from the sideslip on top of whatever roll the ailerons themselves commanded. Coordinated rudder use is what prevents this sideslip — and the resulting secondary roll effect — from developing in the first place.

question: Losing an engine on a multi-engine aircraft with wing-mounted engines typically produces not just a yaw but also a roll, mainly because:

options.text: The resulting yaw creates a sideslip, and the aircraft's own dihedral effect then rolls it in response to that sideslip
Engine failure has no aerodynamic effect beyond the loss of thrust itself
The roll is caused directly by the propeller stopping, with no aerodynamic link to yaw
Roll and yaw are always completely independent of one another on any aircraft

explanation: Asymmetric thrust yaws the aircraft toward the dead engine, and that yaw produces a sideslip; the aircraft's own dihedral effect then responds to that sideslip with a rolling moment — which is why an engine failure is felt, and must be corrected, as a combined yaw-and-roll event rather than pure yaw alone.

question: The general tendency for a yaw disturbance to produce a roll, and for a roll disturbance to produce a yaw, on the same aircraft is known as:

options.text: Lateral-directional coupling
Longitudinal stability
Compressibility
Ground effect

explanation: Because dihedral effect links sideslip to roll, and because a rolling wing produces differential lift and drag that can induce yaw, the roll and yaw axes are never fully independent on a real aircraft — this cross-linkage, seen in phenomena from adverse yaw to Dutch roll to spiral instability, is what "lateral-directional coupling" refers to.

question: An aircraft with high wing loading and low aspect ratio tends to show:

options.text: A more pronounced, sometimes less well damped Dutch roll tendency than a lighter, higher aspect ratio design
No Dutch roll tendency at all, regardless of wing loading
Improved spiral stability as a direct and automatic result of high wing loading
Identical lateral-directional characteristics to any other configuration

explanation: Wing loading and aspect ratio both influence the balance of inertial and aerodynamic forces behind Dutch roll, and aircraft with high wing loading and low aspect ratio (often swept-wing jets) frequently show a more noticeable, sometimes less naturally damped Dutch roll — a major reason such aircraft commonly rely on a yaw damper.

question: A dorsal fin fillet — the fairing blending the fin smoothly into the fuselage — mainly helps directional stability by:

options.text: Delaying the fin's own loss of effectiveness (a form of local stall) at large sideslip angles, maintaining a useful restoring moment further into the sideslip range
Increasing the fin's effectiveness only at very small sideslip angles
Reducing the fin's total area
Having no aerodynamic function, purely a styling feature

explanation: At large sideslip angles, the fin can begin to separate and lose effectiveness much like a wing approaching its own stall. A dorsal fin fillet's shape helps generate a stabilising vortex that keeps flow attached to the fin further into the sideslip range, extending the sideslip angle at which useful directional stability is retained.

question: "Rudder-free" directional stability, as distinct from "rudder-fixed" stability, accounts for:

options.text: The rudder being left free to float aerodynamically rather than held rigidly at a set position, which can change the fin/rudder combination's effective stabilising contribution
An aircraft with no rudder installed at all
Only the ailerons, never the rudder
A rudder that has been mechanically disconnected from the pedals

explanation: Exactly parallel to the stick-fixed/stick-free distinction in longitudinal stability, rudder-fixed directional stability assumes the rudder is locked in position, while rudder-free stability lets it float freely and align aerodynamically with the local airflow — a difference that can genuinely change the fin/rudder assembly's net stabilising contribution.

question: A ventral fin — a fixed surface extending below the aft fuselage — contributes to directional stability mainly by:

options.text: Adding fin area below the fuselage, which is especially useful at high angles of attack where the upper fin's effectiveness may be reduced
Replacing the need for a vertical fin entirely
Only functioning while the landing gear is extended
Reducing the aircraft's overall directional stability

explanation: At high angles of attack, the fuselage or wing wake can shield part of the upper fin, reducing its effectiveness. A ventral fin adds directional-stabilising area below the fuselage, in a position often less affected by that shielding, helping maintain adequate directional stability exactly when the upper fin alone might not be enough.

question: During a crosswind takeoff roll, an aircraft's natural weathercock (directional) stability tends to:

options.text: Turn the aircraft's nose toward the direction the wind is coming from, requiring rudder correction to track the runway centerline
Turn the nose directly away from the wind, with no pilot input needed
Have no effect at all while the aircraft is on the ground
Only appear once the aircraft is airborne

explanation: The same fin-driven weathercock effect that stabilises the aircraft in the air also acts on the ground: a crosswind striking the fin from one side tends to yaw the nose into the wind, requiring active rudder correction throughout the takeoff roll to keep the aircraft tracking straight down the runway.

question: Spiral instability, where it exists, is usually considered a relatively mild handling concern mainly because it:

options.text: Typically develops very slowly, described by a long time constant, giving the pilot ample time to notice and correct the increasing bank with a small aileron input
Develops instantly, with no time for the pilot to react
Is always a rapid, oscillatory motion rather than a slow drift
Cannot occur on any certified aircraft

explanation: Spiral divergence is characterised by a long time constant — bank angle increases only gradually over many seconds — which is quite different from a fast, oscillatory mode like Dutch roll. This slow onset gives a pilot ample opportunity to notice the developing bank and correct it easily, which is why mild spiral instability is often accepted in certification even though it is, strictly, an instability.

question: An aircraft with very strong dihedral effect (strong lateral stability) can present a design trade-off in that:

options.text: Any sideslip from adverse yaw or a gust produces a correspondingly larger, more noticeable rolling response, which can demand more active rudder coordination from the pilot
Strong dihedral effect always makes an aircraft easier to fly with no downside
It eliminates the need for ailerons entirely
It has no relationship to adverse yaw or rudder use at all

explanation: Because dihedral effect converts sideslip into roll, an aircraft with very strong lateral stability responds more vigorously to any sideslip — including the momentary sideslip from adverse yaw — which can make coordinated rudder use more important, not less, on such an aircraft.

question: Fitting wingtip fuel tanks tends to affect an aircraft's lateral dynamics mainly by:

options.text: Increasing roll inertia, since the added mass sits at the greatest possible distance from the roll axis, generally slowing roll response
Reducing roll inertia to essentially zero
Having no effect on roll inertia, only on pitch
Always improving roll rate

explanation: Because roll inertia depends heavily on how far mass sits from the roll axis, adding fuel tanks right at the wingtips — the furthest point from that axis — increases roll inertia disproportionately to the actual weight added, generally slowing the aircraft's roll response compared with the same fuel carried closer to the fuselage.

question: Compared with its dominant role in longitudinal stability, the aircraft's center of gravity position along the fuselage generally has:

options.text: Much less direct effect on lateral and directional static stability, which are governed mainly by wing dihedral/sweep and fin design rather than fore-aft CG position
Exactly the same dominant role in lateral-directional stability as it does in longitudinal stability
No effect whatsoever on any aspect of the aircraft's handling
A greater effect on lateral-directional stability than on longitudinal stability

explanation: Longitudinal static stability depends directly on how far the CG sits ahead of the neutral point along the fuselage, but lateral and directional stability are governed mainly by geometric factors — dihedral, sweep, fin size and position — that are comparatively insensitive to the small fore-aft CG shifts that matter so much for pitch stability.

question: A single-engine propeller aircraft often needs a small, built-in aileron rigging bias or trim setting at cruise power mainly to counter:

options.text: The steady rolling tendency from torque reaction, distinct from any fuel imbalance between the tanks
A crosswind that is always present regardless of conditions
The aircraft's weight alone, with no relationship to the engine
Compressibility effects at cruise power

explanation: Torque reaction produces a steady rolling tendency toward one side at cruise power, independent of any fuel imbalance between the wing tanks, and many single-engine aircraft are rigged with a small built-in aileron offset — or use trim — specifically to counter this steady torque-driven roll.

question: The dihedral-like stabilising contribution from wing sweepback is:

options.text: Proportional to the wing's lift coefficient, so it is weaker at high speed/low CL cruise and stronger at low speed/high CL approach
Completely independent of lift coefficient or angle of attack
Only present at supersonic speed
Strongest at zero lift coefficient

explanation: Sweep's lateral-stabilising effect arises from the difference in effective span (and lift) between the forward and trailing wing during a sideslip, and that lift difference scales with the overall lift coefficient being flown — making the effect comparatively weak in fast, low-CL cruise and considerably stronger in slow, high-CL approach or climb.

question: Dutch roll tends to be less well damped, and therefore more noticeable, at high cruise altitude mainly because:

options.text: The thinner air reduces aerodynamic damping forces relative to the aircraft's inertia, compared with the denser air lower down
Thinner air always improves aerodynamic damping
Dutch roll can only occur above 30,000 feet
Altitude has no bearing on Dutch roll damping at all

explanation: Aerodynamic damping forces depend on air density, which falls with altitude, while the aircraft's mass and inertia stay the same. This shifts the balance toward less-damped oscillation at high altitude, which is a major reason Dutch roll is often most noticeable — and yaw dampers most valued — during high-altitude cruise.

subtopic: Manual Handling of Spiral vs Dutch Roll
question: A pilot can generally correct spiral divergence far more easily by hand than Dutch roll mainly because:

options.text: Spiral divergence develops slowly enough for an occasional small aileron input to correct, while Dutch roll's rapid oscillation is often too fast for a human pilot to damp effectively without automatic assistance
Dutch roll develops so slowly that no correction is ever needed
Spiral divergence cannot be corrected by a pilot under any circumstances
The two modes require exactly the same corrective technique

explanation: Spiral divergence's long time constant leaves plenty of time for an occasional, small aileron correction, while Dutch roll's oscillation is often fast enough that a pilot's own reaction time and control inputs can lag behind or even inadvertently reinforce it — which is exactly why an automatic yaw damper, rather than pilot skill alone, is the standard solution for Dutch roll.

question: A vertical fin of relatively low aspect ratio, common on many aircraft, tends to show:

options.text: A gentler, more gradual loss of effectiveness at high sideslip angles than a higher aspect ratio fin would show
A sharper, more abrupt stall at high sideslip than a high aspect ratio fin
No stalling behaviour of any kind, regardless of sideslip
Exactly the same behaviour as a high aspect ratio fin in every respect

explanation: Just as a low aspect ratio wing tends to stall more gently and progressively than a high aspect ratio one, a low aspect ratio fin — common on many designs — tends to lose effectiveness gradually as sideslip increases rather than abruptly, contributing to more benign high-sideslip and post-stall handling characteristics.

question: During the landing rollout in a crosswind, weathercock stability can contribute to a hazard, particularly on a tailwheel aircraft, because:

options.text: The aircraft's natural tendency to yaw into wind, combined with reduced rudder authority as speed decreases, can produce a swerve toward the upwind side if not actively controlled
Weathercock stability disappears completely once the aircraft has landed
It only ever helps keep the aircraft perfectly straight with no pilot input needed
It has no relationship to ground handling of any kind

explanation: The same weathercock tendency that helps in flight can work against the pilot on the ground: as speed (and therefore rudder authority) falls during the landing rollout, the aircraft's tendency to yaw into a crosswind can overcome the available rudder correction, producing a swerve — a classic contributor to a tailwheel aircraft ground loop if not anticipated and corrected.

question: One aerodynamic factor behind a multi-engine aircraft's minimum control speed, VMCA, is that:

options.text: The fin and rudder combination has a maximum effective sideslip angle, beyond which it stalls and directional control is lost, regardless of how much rudder is applied
The fin can generate an unlimited amount of sideforce at any sideslip angle
VMCA is determined purely by engine power, with no aerodynamic component at all
The fin never contributes to VMCA in any way

explanation: Like a wing, the fin and rudder combination can only generate sideforce up to a limiting sideslip angle before it, too, separates and loses effectiveness. VMCA is reached when full rudder deflection can no longer hold the aircraft straight against asymmetric thrust — partly because the required sideslip angle approaches this aerodynamic limit of the fin itself.

question: On a T-tail aircraft, the horizontal tailplane mounted at the top of the fin can improve the fin's own effectiveness by acting as:

options.text: An end-plate, reducing losses at the fin's tip and effectively increasing the fin's aerodynamic aspect ratio and efficiency
A device that always reduces the fin's effectiveness
A replacement for the fin, making the fin itself unnecessary
A surface with no aerodynamic interaction with the fin at all

explanation: Much like a wingtip device reduces losses at a wingtip, the horizontal tailplane sitting atop a T-tail's fin blocks the spillage of high-pressure air around the fin's own tip, acting as an end-plate that improves the fin's effective aspect ratio and directional-stabilising efficiency for a given fin area.

question: Compared with an aircraft with wing-mounted engines, one with engines mounted on the aft fuselage generally has, following an engine failure:

options.text: A smaller yawing moment from the remaining engine's asymmetric thrust, since the engines sit closer to the aircraft's centerline
A larger yawing moment, since aft-mounted engines are always further from the centerline
Exactly the same yawing moment regardless of engine placement
No yawing moment at all from an engine failure

explanation: Because aft fuselage-mounted engines sit much closer to the aircraft's centerline than wing-mounted ones, the moment arm for asymmetric thrust following an engine failure is considerably shorter, generally producing a smaller yawing moment — one of the handling advantages sometimes cited for rear-engined and T-tail configurations.

question: "Rudder lock" describes a condition in which:

options.text: At a large sideslip angle, aerodynamic forces can hold the rudder hard against its stop, requiring significant pilot force to bring it back toward neutral
The rudder is mechanically bolted in place and cannot move at all
It only ever happens at zero sideslip
It describes a normal, desirable rudder characteristic with no associated hazard

explanation: At a sufficiently large sideslip angle, the aerodynamic force on the rudder can overcome the pilot's ability to hold it away from full deflection, effectively "locking" it against its travel limit until sideslip is reduced — a real historical handling concern that careful fin and dorsal fin design, among other things, is intended to avoid.

question: Ice accumulating unevenly between the two wings, thicker on one side than the other, can require rudder trim correction because:

options.text: The extra drag on the more heavily iced wing yaws the aircraft toward that side, distinct from any rolling tendency from an uneven weight distribution
Ice never produces any asymmetric aerodynamic effect
Only aileron trim, never rudder trim, is ever affected by icing
Uneven icing always produces exactly the same effect as a fuel imbalance

explanation: Beyond any weight-related rolling tendency, ice that accumulates more heavily on one wing adds extra drag on that side specifically, yawing the aircraft toward the more heavily contaminated wing — a distinct, drag-driven directional effect that may call for rudder trim correction alongside anything needed in roll.

question: At a sufficiently large combined angle of attack and sideslip, the vertical fin itself can:

options.text: Stall in essentially the same way a wing does, with airflow separating from it and its restoring sideforce falling away
Never lose effectiveness under any combination of angle of attack and sideslip
Only fail structurally, never aerodynamically
Always become more effective as sideslip increases without limit

explanation: Like any other aerodynamic surface, the fin has a critical angle beyond which the airflow over it separates and its ability to generate a restoring sideforce collapses — a genuine "fin stall", distinct from the wing's own stall, that is a real factor in high-sideslip handling, spin behaviour and VMCA.
